# Adjudication Task — Chapter 575

## Korean source

```text
  1|＃575화
  2|
  3|
  4|
  5|굳이 눈으로 확인할 필요도, 달려가 맥을 짚을 필요도 없었다.
  6|
  7|푸른 화염에 휩싸인 창날이 크라켄의 몸뚱어리를 파고든 순간, 나는 깨달았다.
  8|
  9|‘끝났다.’
 10|
 11|서걱! 퍼엉!
 12|
 13|절삭. 동시에 내부로부터 일어난 화기(火氣)의 폭발.
 14|
 15|세로 길이만 십여 미터에 달하는 괴수의 머리가 풍선처럼 터져 나가고, 해수면 위로 미처 증발하지 않은 푸른 핏물이 소나기처럼 쏟아져 내린다.
 16|
 17|그리고 다음 순간.
 18|
 19|콰아아아-
 20|
 21|마침내 쓰러지는 크라켄의 거대한 동체와 함께, 맑은 종소리가 귓가를 파고들었다.
 22|
 23|띠링.
 24|
 25|
 26|
 27|- [Lv.140 ‘검은 바다의 왕’ 크라켄]을 처치했습니다!
 28|
 29|- 대량의 경험치를 획득했습니다!
 30|
 31|- [만독지환]이 체내의 모든 독을 해독했습니다!
 32|
 33|- 상태 이상, [중독]이 사라집니다!
 34|
 35|- 상태 이상, [마비]가 사라집니다!
 36|
 37|
 38|
 39|크라켄을 처치했다는 시스템 알림에도, 내 입 안은 모래를 씹은 것처럼 꺼끌거렸다.
 40|
 41|‘제기랄.’
 42|
 43|살렸어야 했다. 어떻게든 살려서 배후의 진짜 정체를 알아냈어야 했다.
 44|
 45|하지만 한순간의 방심은 돌이킬 수 없는 결과를 불러 왔고, 크라켄은 풀리지 않는 문제를 남기고 죽었다.
 46|
 47|만약 놈이 곧장 나를 공격했더라면 충분한 가능성이 있었겠지만…….
 48|
 49|‘이미 늦었어.’
 50|
 51|크라켄은 생각 이상으로 영리했다.
 52|
 53|놈은 중독된 내가 자신보다 강하다는 것을 알고 있었고, 결코 도망칠 수 없다는 사실도 인지하고 있었다.
 54|
 55|그렇기에 나 대신 생존자들을 노렸을 것이다. 사로잡히느니 죽기 위해서.
 56|
 57|그리고 이런 크라켄의 마지막 발악 앞에서, 내게 남은 선택지는 하나밖에 없었다.
 58|
 59|“……후.”
 60|
 61|나는 해수면 위에 반쯤 잠긴 크라켄의 사체를 보며 한숨을 내쉬었다.
 62|
 63|어쩔 수 없는 선택이었다. 단 일격에 놈을 죽이지 않았다면, 당장 눈앞에서 누군가가 죽었을 테니까.
 64|
 65|대(大)를 위한 소(小)의 희생이라는 말도 겉만 번드르르할 뿐. 결국 그 본질은 희생이며 막을 힘이 있음에도 개죽음을 방관하는 것밖에 안 된다.
 66|
 67|‘끝까지 방심하지 말았어야 했는데…….’
 68|
 69|이미 엎질러진 물이다.
 70|
 71|끝내 배후를 밝혀 내지 못했다는 사실에 대해 불안감과 후회가 드는 건 사실이지만, 그렇다고 해서 크라켄을 죽인 것을 후회하지는 않는다.
 72|
 73|내 선택으로 살아난 사람들이 있으니까.
 74|
 75|“여, 여기요! 여기 좀 살려 주세요!”
 76|
 77|“쿨럭! 제발 우리 애 좀……!”
 78|
 79|“엄마! 엄마아아아!”
 80|
 81|최대한 멀리 떨어져 싸운 덕분일까.
 82|
 83|내가 미처 도착하기도 전에 수백의 사상자가 발생했지만, 아직 구조를 기다리는 생존자들의 숫자가 더 많다.
 84|
 85|출렁이는 바다와 붕괴한 광안대교에서 들려오는 사람들의 간절한 외침에, 나는 억지로 피로를 털어내며 신형을 날렸다.
 86|
 87|쐐애애액!
 88|
 89|비릿하고도 상쾌한 바다 냄새가 콧속 깊숙이 스며든다.
 90|
 91|나는 한 줄기의 돌풍이 되어 수면 위를 가로질렀다.
 92|
 93|둥둥 떠 있는 크라켄의 사체를 넘어 사람들에게 도달한 나는 그들을 빠르게 끌어올리며 당부했다.
 94|
 95|“위험하니까 모두 여기 계셔야 합니다. 여력이 있으신 분들은 우선 저와 함께 다른 분들을 구해 주시고요.”
 96|
 97|그나마 멀쩡해 보이는 청년이 물을 뱉어 내며 입을 열었다.
 98|
 99|“콜록. 그, 그래도 다른 곳으로 도망쳐야…….”
100|
101|“도망이요?”
102|
103|“예, 예에.”
104|
105|나는 손을 들어 어딘가를 가리켰다. 사방에 빽빽한 빌딩 숲 사이로 피어오르는 검은 연기.
106|
107|평범한 민간인인 이들은 들을 수 없겠지만, 극도로 감각이 발달한 나는 이미 알고 있었다.
108|
109|- 시시시시싯!
110|
111|- 탱커! 삼보 전진!
112|
113|- 건물! 건물이 무너집니다! 민간인들이 위험합니다!
114|
115|- 으아아악!
116|
117|구구구궁! 콰앙!
118|
119|희미하게 들려오는 비명과 굉음. 얼마 떨어지지 않은 곳에서 인간과 몬스터의 시가전(市街戰)이 벌어지고 있다는 증거다.
120|
121|그것도 인근 곳곳에서 동시다발적으로.
122|
123|“사방에 몬스터가 기다리고 있는데, 가실래요?”
124|
125|“……아뇨. 여기 있겠습니다.”
126|
127|그나마 빨리 알아먹어서 다행이군.
128|
129|비록 크라켄이 죽었다 해도 모든 것이 끝난 것은 아니다.
130|
131|이 혼란을 완전히 잠재우기 위해서는, 오늘 하루를 아주 바쁘게 보내야 할 것 같았다.
132|
133|쐐애애액, 펑!
134|
135|수면을 박차고 솟구치는 내 모습을, 생존자들이 넋 나간 시선으로 바라보았다.
136|
137|
138|
139|* * *
140|
141|
142|
143|사람이라면 누구나 식사를 한다.
144|
145|하지만 함께 식사하는 사람이 누구냐에 따라, 그리고 장소에 따라 격식이 달라진다는 것은 부정할 수 없는 사실이다.
146|
147|그런 의미에서, 단 두 사람이 마주한 오늘의 식사는 상당한 격식이 있었다.
148|
149|느지막이 시작한 아침 식사는 두런두런 오가는 이야기와 함께 장장 두 시간이나 이어졌고, 어느덧 새하얀 식탁보에는 예쁘게 장식된 수정과가 올라왔다.
150|
151|“곧 설이라 떡국을 준비한 건데…… 어떻게, 식사가 우리 최 팀장님 입맛에 맞으셨는지 모르겠습니다.”
152|
153|정중하면서도 부드러운 목소리에, 냅킨으로 입을 문지른 최민우가 입을 열었다.
154|
155|“대통령님께서 신경 써 주신 덕분인지, 맛이 아주 훌륭했습니다.”
156|
157|“하하. 그렇다니 다행입니다.”
158|
159|맞은편에 앉아 있던 중년인, 백한성 대통령이 사람 좋은 웃음을 지으며 말을 이었다.
160|
161|“요새 워낙 바쁘셔서 통 끼니를 챙기지 못할 것 같길래. 내 우리 청와대 조리장한테 신신당부했습니다. 중요한 손님이니까 특별히 신경 써 달라고.”
162|
163|중요한 손님이라는 표현은 결코 빈말이 아니었다.
164|
165|청와대 조찬(朝餐)에 초대받았다는 것만으로도 상당한 힘을 지닌 유력 인사라는 뜻이지만, 단둘이 하는 식사는 그 의미가 남다르다.
166|
167|이는 백한성 대통령이 그만큼 최민우를 중요시하고 있다는 뜻이었다.
168|
169|“잘 먹으니까 보기 좋아요. 뿌듯하기도 하고.”
170|
171|최민우가 가볍게 고개를 숙였다.
172|
173|“감사합니다. 그래도 대통령님께서 생각하시는 것만큼 굶고 다니지는 않는데, 괜히 걱정을 끼쳐 드린 것 같군요.”
174|
175|“아, 그렇습니까? 하긴 팀장님도 전속 셰프가 있겠군요.”
176|
177|“아닙니다. 요즘은 따로 챙겨 주시는 분이 계셔서요.”
178|
179|“따로 식사를 챙겨 주시는 분이라면…… 아, 혹시?”
180|
181|최민우가 작게 고개를 끄덕였다.
182|
183|“진태경 씨의 어머니께서 식사를 차려 주십니다.”
184|
185|“허어, 모친께서 직접?”
186|
187|“예. 도리가 아닌 것 같아 거절해도 워낙 완고하셔서.”
188|
189|백한성 대통령은 작은 탄성을 흘렸다.
190|
191|진태경의 가족이 최민우의 저택에서 임시로 머무르고 있다는 이야기는 이미 알고 있던 사실이었지만, 직접 당사자의 입을 통해 들으니 의미가 남달랐다.
192|
193|‘식사까지 챙겨 줄 정도라면…… 생각했던 것 이상으로 친밀하군.’
194|
195|진태경과 최민우. 최민우와 진태경.
196|
197|이 두 사람은 백한성 대통령의 입장에서는 결코 놓을 수 없는 대어(大魚)인 동시에 막강한 영향력을 행사하는 아레스 길드를 억누를 수 있는 유일한 대책이기도 했다.
198|
199|엄청난 위상을 지닌 진태경과, 천태민의 외손자이자 유일한 혈육인 최민우.
200|
201|이 두 사람과 함께한다면 더욱 높은 자리에 오를 수 있다.
202|
203|대한민국 최연소 대통령에 이어, 바뀐 법률에 따라 최초의 재선(再選) 대통령이 될 가능성도 충분한 것이다.
204|
205|‘무슨 수를 써서라도 저 둘만큼은 반드시 내 사람으로 만들어야 한다.’
206|
207|다분히 정치적인 생각을 떠올리는 백한성 대통령과 달리, 최민우는 커피를 마시며 완전히 다른 생각을 하고 있었다.
208|
209|‘오늘 해 주시겠다고 한 저녁 메뉴가 아마…… 김치찌개였나.’
210|
211|이상한 일이다. 이제 막 식사를 끝마쳤음에도 위장이 텅 빈 것 같은 공복감이라니.
212|
213|국내 최고의 한식 명인이라는 청와대 조리장이 심혈을 기울여 만든 떡국보다, 진태경의 모친이 만든 김치찌개가 먹고 싶었다.
214|
215|요즘은 찾아보기 힘든 압력밥솥으로 만든 고슬고슬한 흰 쌀밥에 푹 익은 돼지고기와 김치.
216|
217|그리고 한 식탁에 옹기종기 앉아 정신없이 수저를 놀리는 사람들.
218|
219|‘음.’
220|
221|최민우는 어느새 입맛을 다시고 있는 자신의 모습에, 문득 무언가를 깨닫고 실소를 흘렸다.
222|
223|‘그래. 그런 거였군.’
224|
225|그는 떡국도, 김치찌개도 그리 좋아하지 않는다.
226|
227|저녁 식사가 기다려지는 이유 역시 그녀의 요리 솜씨가 청와대 조리장보다 좋아서가 아니다.
228|
229|그저…… 그 자리가 좋았다. 따뜻한 밥이, 따뜻한 사람들과 함께 하는 그 자리가.
230|
231|‘집.’
232|
233|그리고 가족.
234|
235|최민우에게 있어 그 두 개의 단어는, 지금 앉아 있는 의자보다 키가 작았을 때 잃어버린 것이었다. 이제 두 번 다시 되찾을 수 없으리라 생각했던 무언가.
236|
237|‘아니. 가족이라면 아직 한 사람이 남아 있긴 하지.’
238|
239|인류를 구한 영웅이자 살아 있는 구세주.
240|
241|하지만 당신의 가족만은 지키지 못했던 한 사람.
242|
243|최민우는 기억도 나지 않는 외조부와의 마지막 만남을 떠올리며 내심 중얼거렸다.
244|
245|‘이제 곧…… 다시 뵐 수 있겠군요.’
246|
247|수십 년간 두문불출한 외조부를 떠올리자 의미를 알 수 없는 감정이 문득 고개를 들었다.
248|
249|평소와는 다른 최민우의 분위기를 눈치챈 백한성 대통령이 의문을 담아 물었다.
250|
251|“어디 불편하신 데라도?”
252|
253|“아. 아닙니다. 아무것도.”
254|
255|“허허. 그렇군요. 그럼 이제 식사도 끝마쳤겠다, 팀장님과 긴히 논의할 사항이 있는…….”
256|
257|벌컥.
258|
259|그러나 백한성 대통령의 말은 끝까지 이어지지 못했다.
260|
261|노크도 없이 들어온 보좌관의 모습을 확인한 그가 눈살을 찌푸렸다.
262|
263|“아무도 들어오지 말라고 했을 텐데.”
264|
265|“죄송합니다. 가급적이면 그러려고 했는데 연락을 받지 않으셔서…….”
266|
267|“연락? 그야 당연히 무음으로 해 뒀지.”
268|
269|중요한 이야기가 오가는 자리. 서로의 위치를 생각해 보면 스마트폰을 꺼내는 건 상당한 결례였다.
270|
271|“후욱, 죄송합니다. 하지만 워낙 급한 일이라.”
272|
273|거칠게 몰아쉬는 숨과 이마에 맺혀 있는 땀.
274|
275|보좌관의 모습에서 심상치 않은 기색을 느낀 최민우는 정장 안감에 넣어 둔 스마트폰을 꺼냈다.
276|
277|김 집사에게서 걸려온 십여 통의 부재중 전화와 쌓여 있는 문자.
278|
279|마음 깊은 곳으로부터 불길함이 솟구쳤다.
280|
281|‘설마?’
282|
283|그리고 문자의 내용을 확인한 순간, 잘 정돈된 눈썹이 움찔 떨렸다.
284|
285|
286|
287|〈 김 집사님
288|
289|
290|
291|김 집사님
292|
293|긴급 부산 몬스터 웨이브 발생
294|

With those two on his side, Baek could rise still higher. After becoming the youngest president in Korea’s history, he might well become the first to win reelection under the amended law.

[P89]
*Whatever it takes, I have to bring them both over to my side.*

[P90]
While President Baek’s thoughts ran to politics, Choi Minwoo sipped his coffee and thought about something else entirely.

[P91]
*She said she was making dinner tonight… Kimchi stew, was it?*

[P92]
Strange. He had just finished breakfast, yet his stomach felt empty.

[P93]
He wanted Jin Taekyung’s mother’s kimchi stew more than the tteokguk the Blue House head chef—a master of Korean cuisine—had prepared with such care.

[P94]
Fluffy white rice from a pressure cooker of a kind rarely seen these days. Pork cooked until tender, and well-aged kimchi.

[P95]
And people sitting close together around one table, too busy eating to put down their spoons.

[P96]
*Hmm.*

[P97]
Choi Minwoo caught himself smacking his lips and gave a quiet, rueful laugh.

[P98]
*So that’s what it is.*

[P99]
He wasn’t particularly fond of tteokguk or kimchi stew. Nor was he looking forward to dinner because her cooking was better than the Blue House chef’s.

[P100]
He simply liked being there. The warm food, shared with warm people.

[P101]
*Home.*

[P102]
And family.

[P103]
Choi Minwoo had lost both before he was as tall as the chair he sat in now. He had thought he could never have them again.

[P104]
*No. I do still have one family member.*

[P105]
A hero who had saved humanity. A living savior.

[P106]
But a man who had been unable to protect his own family.

[P107]
Choi Minwoo thought of the last time he had seen his maternal grandfather—a meeting he could no longer remember.

[P108]
*Soon… I’ll see you again.*

[P109]
At the thought of the grandfather who had shut himself away for decades, a feeling he couldn’t name rose within him.

[P110]
President Baek noticed the change in his expression.

[P111]
“Is something troubling you?”

[P112]
“Ah. No. It’s nothing.”

[P113]
“Ha-ha. I see. Well, now that we’ve finished eating, there’s something important I’d like to discuss with you, Team Leader—”

[P114]
The door flew open.

[P115]
President Baek stopped mid-sentence. He frowned at the aide who had entered without knocking.

[P116]
“I thought I told everyone not to come in.”

[P117]
“I’m sorry. I tried to avoid it, but you weren’t answering…”

[P118]
“Answering? Of course not. My phone’s on silent.”

[P119]
With an important conversation under way, taking out a smartphone would have been discourteous, given who was at the table.

[P120]
“Huff… I’m sorry. But it’s urgent.”

[P121]
The aide was breathing hard, sweat beading on his forehead.

[P122]
Sensing something was wrong, Choi Minwoo took the smartphone from inside his suit jacket. He had more than ten missed calls from Butler Kim and a string of text messages.

[P123]
Dread rose in him.

[P124]
*Don’t tell me…*

[P125]
He opened the messages. One of his neatly groomed eyebrows twitched.

[P126]
> Butler Kim
>
> Butler Kim
>
> Emergency Monster Wave in Busan
>
> Extra-large named monster sighted
>
> Young Master, where are you?
>
> Young Mster

[P127]
The messages were from Butler Kim. They were short, but there was nothing small about the news.

[P128]
*A Monster Wave? In Busan?*

[P129]
Busan was Korea’s second-largest city, home to millions. An extra-large named monster could cause an enormous loss of life just by doing a forward roll.

[P130]
And what the aide said next made matters worse.

[P131]
“The emergency alert was delayed by a little over ten minutes. The Monster Wave happened so suddenly, and the Gate management office and the surrounding facilities were all destroyed…”

[P132]
“You idiot! Do you hear yourself?”

[P133]
“I-I’m sorry.”

[P134]
Sweat poured down the aide’s face as he continued.

[P135]
“But according to a report from one minute ago, the extra-large named monster has been subdued. Hunter Jin Taekyung happened to arrive at the scene…”

[P136]
“What? Are you certain?”

[P137]
“Yes. The remaining monsters are being dealt with, and survivors are being rescued.”

[P138]
“…Phew. At least there’s that.”

[P139]
President Baek let out a sigh of relief. Choi Minwoo rose without hesitation.

[P140]
The worst of the immediate crisis might have passed, but this was no time to sit and talk.

[P141]
“I’ll be going, Mr. President.”

[P142]
“Of course. We’ll speak another time.”

[P143]
They exchanged brief farewells. Choi Minwoo had just left the Blue House when—

[P144]
*Bzzzzzt.*

[P145]
His phone, now turned back on, vibrated forcefully.

[P146]
Team Leader Choi thought he knew who was calling and answered at once.

[P147]
“Yes, Butler Kim. I’m on my way ri—”

[P148]
—It’s me.

[P149]
“…!”

[P150]
Choi Minwoo stopped dead.

[P151]
Song Cheonwoo’s aged voice came through the phone.

[P152]
—We need to talk. It’s urgent.

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.

*If she’s even cooking for him… They’re closer than I thought.*

[P85]
Jin Taekyung and Choi Minwoo. Choi Minwoo and Jin Taekyung.

[P86]
To President Baek, they were two enormously valuable men he could not afford to lose. They were also his only means of keeping the immensely influential Ares Guild in check.

[P87]
Jin Taekyung, with his extraordinary standing. Choi Minwoo, Cheon Taemin’s maternal grandson and only living blood relative.

[P88]
With those two on his side, Baek could rise still higher. After becoming the youngest president in Korea’s history, he might well become the first to win reelection under the amended law.

[P89]
*Whatever it takes, I have to bring them both over to my side.*

[P90]
While President Baek’s thoughts ran to politics, Choi Minwoo sipped his coffee and thought about something else entirely.

[P91]
*She said she was making dinner tonight… Kimchi stew, was it?*

[P92]
Strange. He had just finished breakfast, yet his stomach felt empty.

[P93]
He wanted Jin Taekyung’s mother’s kimchi stew more than the tteokguk the Blue House head chef—a master of Korean cuisine—had prepared with such care.

[P94]
Fluffy white rice from a pressure cooker of a kind rarely seen these days. Pork cooked until tender, and well-aged kimchi.

[P95]
And people sitting close together around one table, too busy eating to put down their spoons.

[P96]
*Hmm.*

[P97]
Choi Minwoo caught himself smacking his lips and gave a quiet, rueful laugh.

[P98]
*So that’s what it is.*

[P99]
He wasn’t particularly fond of tteokguk or kimchi stew. Nor was he looking forward to dinner because her cooking was better than the Blue House chef’s.

[P100]
He simply liked being there. The warm food, shared with warm people.

[P101]
*Home.*

[P102]
And family.

[P103]
Choi Minwoo had lost both before he was as tall as the chair he sat in now. He had thought he could never have them again.

[P104]
*No. I do still have one family member.*

[P105]
A hero who had saved humanity. A living savior.

[P106]
But a man who had been unable to protect his own family.

[P107]
Choi Minwoo thought of the last time he had seen his maternal grandfather—a meeting he could no longer remember.

[P108]
*Soon… I’ll see you again.*

[P109]
At the thought of the grandfather who had shut himself away for decades, a feeling he couldn’t name rose within him.

[P110]

[P111]
“Is something troubling you?”

[P112]

[P113]

[P114]
The door flew open.

[P115]

[P116]

[P117]

[P118]

[P119]

[P120]
“Huff… I’m sorry. But it’s urgent.”

[P121]
The aide was breathing hard, sweat beading on his forehead.

[P122]

[P123]
Dread rose in him.

[P124]
*Don’t tell me…*

[P125]
He opened the messages. One of his neatly groomed eyebrows twitched.

[P126]
> Butler Kim
>
> Butler Kim
>
> Emergency Monster Wave in Busan
>
> Extra-large named monster sighted
>
> Young Master, where are you?
>
> Young Mster

[P127]

[P128]
*A Monster Wave? In Busan?*

[P129]

[P130]

[P132]

[P133]

[P134]

[P135]

[P136]

[P137]

[P138]

[P139]

[P140]

[P141]

[P142]

[P143]

[P144]
*Bzzzzzt.*

[P145]

[P146]

[P147]

[P148]
—It’s me.

[P149]
“…!”

[P150]

[P151]

[P152]

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

Do not `REPAIR` a working SOL line. Do not invent a third style because you prefer it.

For `REPAIR`, write the smallest complete replacement needed for that hunk. It must be natural English and fully source-faithful.

## Glossary

Korean **keys** are binding unless the source uses that string in a different ordinary-language sense. Glossary **English** is not a license for a calque (`presiding chair`). If SOL is a natural recast of the same sense, keep SOL.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.
